column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbdillāh Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Anṣārī (may Allah be pleased with them both) that a man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ,
saying: “Do you think that if I pray the obligatory prayers, fast Ramaḍān, treat the lawful as lawful and the unlawful as unlawful, and do nothing more than that, I will enter Paradise?”
He said: “Yes.” Reported by Muslim. The meaning of “I treat the unlawful as unlawful” is: I avoid it; and the meaning of “I treat the lawful as lawful” is: I do it believing it to be lawful.
In some routes of the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (15), the man who asked is named as al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal.
The questioner's words, “Do you think” (a-raʾayta), mean: Tell me, if I do these things, will I enter Paradise?

The matters about which he asked whether he would enter Paradise if he did them are prayer, fasting, treating the lawful as lawful and treating the unlawful as unlawful. Zakāh and Ḥajj are not mentioned among them. It may be that Ḥajj was not mentioned because it had not yet been made obligatory,

and zakāh was not mentioned because he may have been poor, with no wealth on which to pay zakāh; and it may be that zakāh and Ḥajj are included under treating the lawful as lawful and the unlawful as unlawful.

The hadith mentions carrying out the obligations, but it does not mention recommended acts. Whoever is like this is the one who takes the middle course (muqtaṣid) in the saying of the Exalted: “Then We caused to inherit the Book those We chose of Our servants; among them is he who wrongs himself, among them is he who takes the middle course, and among them is he who is foremost in good deeds by permission of Allah” [Fāṭir 35:32].
Doing the obligations and leaving the unlawful are a cause of entering Paradise, but doing voluntary deeds along with the obligatory ones completes the obligatory ones if one has not done them fully,
as an authentic hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ states, reported by Abū Dāwūd (864), al-Tirmidhī (413) and Ibn Mājah (1425).

Moreover, voluntary deeds are like a fence around the obligatory ones: whoever keeps to them is even more careful to keep the obligatory ones, while whoever is careless about them may be drawn into neglecting the obligatory ones.
The Companions were eager to know the deeds that lead into Paradise.
Deeds are a cause of entering Paradise.
The five prayers are of great importance; a hadith says that they are the central pillar of Islam.
Fasting Ramaḍān is of great importance.
The Muslim treats the lawful as lawful, believing it to be lawful, and avoids the unlawful, believing it to be unlawful.

The hadith shows the falsity of the claim of some Sufis that a person should not worship Allah out of desire for Paradise and fear of the Fire, when Allah has said of His intimate friend [Ibrāhīm]: “And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss” [al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:85].
